clue.text: Moving text from model with no more energy

blocks.note: a model to imitate is a copy to follow
with means together with, plus
what is no more is past
E is the symbol for energy in physics

explanation.surface: An editor shifts a passage of writing taken from a template, too tired to do anything more.
explanation.definitionFit: Copying a passage and pasting it elsewhere is the standard computer way of relocating words in a document.

clue.text: Salad cream could be reimagined in ads this sweet

indicators.note: reimagined means rethought into a new form, so the letters can be rearranged
the salad cream is said to sit inside the word ads, so taking that word away leaves what was rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written; these letters are the wrapping to discard

explanation.surface: An advertiser rebrands a salad dressing as a dessert.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue works backwards: CARAMEL, rearranged and put inside ADS, would make SALAD CREAM, so remove A, D and S and rearrange what is left.
explanation.definitionFit: Caramel is a confection of browned sugar, a kind of candy or toffee eaten as a treat.

clue.text: Bit of butter on bun, ending with different size rounds

indicators.note: the last letter of the bun word is swapped for another one, signalled by a different size

blocks.note: a pat is a small slab of butter
a bread roll is a bun
S for small replaces the final L, which stands for large: a different size

explanation.surface: Someone butters a bun before cutting it into slices of varying size.
explanation.walkthrough: Clothing sizes are marked L for large and S for small, so swapping the last letter of ROLL gives ROLS.
explanation.definitionFit: A police officer's or guard's rounds are the regular circuits walked, which are also called patrols.

clue.text: Spirit character in Tempest that is out to embrace transformation

indicators.note: out says those letters must leave the character's name
to embrace is to hug, so what remains wraps around the next word

blocks.note: Ariel is the airy sprite in Shakespeare's The Tempest
i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, that is
a transformation is a change

explanation.surface: A theatre note about the magical servant in Shakespeare's play who undergoes a metamorphosis.
explanation.walkthrough: Ariel himself is a spirit, so the clue tempts you to stop there; the definition is just the first word.
explanation.definitionFit: An archangel is a high-ranking angel, and angels are heavenly spirits in Christian tradition.

clue.text: Germany will crush any revolutionary protests

indicators.note: something revolutionary turns over, so the word for any is read the other way round

blocks.note: D is the international vehicle code for Germany (Deutschland)
any and some are interchangeable, as in have you any or some

explanation.surface: A threat that the German state will put down any uprisings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Will crush' only places the D hard up against the next piece. DEMOS is the British informal short form of demonstrations.
explanation.definitionFit: Demos is a casual clipping of demonstrations, the public marches and rallies held to object to something.

clue.text: Lay a covering on France’s Route du Sud

indicators.note: from the south means coming upwards, so in a down entry the French road is read bottom to top

blocks.note: taken as written
a mat is a floor covering
rue is the French word for a street or road

explanation.surface: An instruction to resurface a southern French highway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lay' looks like a verb, but it is the adjective meaning not professional, as in a lay preacher.
explanation.definitionFit: Lay as an adjective means non-professional or non-expert, which is exactly what an amateur is.

clue.text: Experiment involving four or six without gravity

indicators.note: involving means including inside, so the number sits within the experiment word

blocks.note: a trial is a test or experiment
Roman four, IV, goes after TR; Roman six, VI, after TRI gives the same letters, hence the or

explanation.surface: A physics test with a handful of samples conducted in zero gravity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without gravity' suggests space science, but gravity here means seriousness.
explanation.definitionFit: Something lacking seriousness or weight is of little importance, which is what trivial means.

clue.text: Shooter that usually puts a smiley face on their target?

definitions.text: Shooter that usually puts a smiley face on their target?

blocks.note: surface reading: a marksman aiming a gun at a target painted with a smiley face

blocks.clueFragment: puts a smiley face on their target
blocks.note: setter's reading: someone who shoots with a camera and gets the subject to grin for the picture

explanation.walkthrough: Shoot is also slang for taking pictures, and the person being pictured is usually asked to say cheese.
explanation.definitionFit: A person taking portraits aims a camera at a subject and typically coaxes them into smiling.

clue.text: One disbelieves quote about Hearts making a comeback

indicators.note: a comeback is a return, so the whole string is read in the opposite direction

blocks.note: to quote a source is to cite it
re means about or concerning
H is the card abbreviation for hearts

explanation.surface: A sports report quoting someone who doubts Hearts, the Edinburgh football club, can recover.
explanation.walkthrough: Hearts is the Scottish football club Heart of Midlothian, which makes the surface about a sporting revival.
explanation.definitionFit: A heretic rejects accepted religious doctrine, someone who refuses to believe the orthodox faith.

clue.text: This person needs a belt or more strapping

blocks.note: the setter speaking of themself
taken as written
a belt is a band or layer, as is a tier

explanation.surface: Someone putting on weight needs to tighten a belt or add another strap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strapping' looks like straps for a belt, but it means burly and well built.
explanation.definitionFit: A strapping person is big and brawny; beefier or meatier describes someone even more muscular.

clue.text: Met drunk in wrong entrance – start of sad events, getting done over

indicators.note: someone drunk staggers about, so the letters of Met lurch out of order
wrong means not in its right form, so the letters of entrance are rearranged
in places one rearranged word inside the other
start of asks only for the opening letter of the next word

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
taken as written, to be rearranged
first letter of sad

explanation.surface: A tipsy police officer stumbles through the wrong doorway, the start of a sorry episode.
explanation.walkthrough: Met is the Metropolitan Police, London's police force, which steers the surface towards a drunken officer.
explanation.definitionFit: Re-enactments are performances staging past happenings again, such as historical battles played out a second time.

clue.text: A fling, then Frenchman’s word is retracted in game of chance

indicators.note: retracted means drawn back, so the whole sequence is read backwards

blocks.note: taken as written
to lob is to fling or toss upwards
mot is French for word

explanation.surface: A man has an affair, then a Frenchman goes back on his promise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fling' reads as a brief romance, but it is a throw. A tombola is a raffle common at British school fairs, where tickets are drawn from a drum.
explanation.definitionFit: A tombola is a lottery-style raffle where prizes are won by drawing numbered tickets from a revolving drum.

clue.text: Electronic bug located after street clean

blocks.note: St is the abbreviation for street
E is a common abbreviation for electronic, as in e-mail
to bug someone is to annoy or rile them

explanation.surface: A listening device found once a road was swept by security.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bug' suggests a hidden microphone, but here it is the verb meaning to irritate.
explanation.definitionFit: Sterile means free from germs and contamination, completely hygienic in the medical sense.

clue.text: Festivities end in brawling, I regret to say

indicators.note: end in asks for the final letter of the word that follows

blocks.note: last letter of brawling
alas is an exclamation of regret

explanation.surface: Sadly, the party ended in a fight.
explanation.definitionFit: Galas are grand celebratory occasions or festive entertainments, such as a charity ball or a swimming gala.

clue.text: Warrior takes 31 days over suppressing sin and evil

indicators.note: over means turned over, so the month abbreviation is read backwards
suppressing means holding down, so the month keeps the other words held inside it

blocks.note: August has 31 days, abbreviated Aug
to err is to sin or go wrong
ill as a noun means harm or evil

explanation.surface: A fighter spends a month away, resisting temptation and wickedness.
explanation.walkthrough: Several months have 31 days; the one that fits is August.
explanation.definitionFit: A guerrilla is an irregular fighter in a small independent band, so a kind of warrior or combatant.

clue.text: Sharp metal ruler to be pulled out?

definitions.text: Sharp metal ruler to be pulled out?

blocks.note: surface reading: a steel measuring rule with a keen edge that someone tugs from a drawer
setter's reading: a blade that the future king had to draw from the stone to prove himself

explanation.walkthrough: 'Ruler' means a measuring stick in the surface but a king in the answer: the legendary sword only the rightful monarch could draw from a stone.
explanation.definitionFit: In Arthurian legend this is the sword that the young Arthur pulled from a stone, proving he should be king.

clue.text: Company with hotel invested in local I used as boozer

indicators.note: used means worked on or exploited, so those letters are rearranged
money invested in a business is put inside it, so the firm goes within the other letters

blocks.note: Co is the abbreviation for company
H is hotel in the NATO phonetic alphabet
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A hotel chain buys into the neighbourhood pub that the speaker uses as a drinking spot.
explanation.walkthrough: A local is a British pub near home, and boozer is also British slang for a pub; here boozer means the drinker instead.
explanation.definitionFit: A boozer is a heavy drinker, someone dependent on drink, which is what an alcoholic is.

clue.text: Somewhere upper-class French ate aubergine parcels

indicators.note: to parcel is to wrap up, so the letters lie wrapped within the preceding words

blocks.note: spans the end of French, all of ate and the start of aubergine

explanation.surface: A posh French diner eats aubergine wrapped in pastry.
explanation.walkthrough: French does double duty: it hides letters and hints that the grand home is a French one.
explanation.definitionFit: A chateau is a grand country house or castle in France, a residence for the aristocracy or wealthy.

clue.text: Revolting, in retreat, time to go south

indicators.note: to go says the time letter leaves, with the compass point taking its place

blocks.note: a hideout is a secluded retreat
T is the abbreviation for time; this is the letter removed
S is the abbreviation for south; this is the letter put in

explanation.surface: An army in rebellion falls back, deciding it is time to head south.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolting' and 'retreat' suggest an uprising in flight, but revolting means disgusting.
explanation.definitionFit: Hideous means extremely ugly or repulsive, so something revolting to look at.

clue.text: What jazz singers can do to keep new is limited

indicators.note: to keep is to hold, so the singing word holds the next letter inside it

blocks.note: scat is improvised wordless jazz singing
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: A remark that jazz vocalists have little room to try anything fresh.
explanation.definitionFit: Scant means barely sufficient or meagre, so present only in a small, restricted amount.

clue.text: Eventually 4 will go north a year

indicators.note: heading north in a down entry means reading upwards, so the earlier answer is turned round

blocks.note: the answer to 4 down
taken as written
Y is the abbreviation for year

explanation.surface: Eventually the protests will move up the country within twelve months.
explanation.definitionFit: Someday means at some unspecified future time, which is what eventually also suggests.

clue.text: Integrated in Singapore, do Malaysians put up with it?

indicators.note: integrated in means built into, so the letters sit inside the words that follow
put up means raised, and in a down entry raising letters reads them bottom to top

blocks.note: spans the last letter of Singapore, all of do and the start of Malaysians

explanation.surface: A question about whether Malaysians integrated into Singapore society can tolerate the situation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put up with it' reads as one phrase meaning tolerate; split it, so 'put up' is the reversal and 'with it' the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A la mode is French for in the fashion, so it means trendy or stylish, which is what with it means.

clue.text: One simply can’t resist house stuffing

definitions.text: One simply can’t resist house stuffing

blocks.note: surface reading: someone who cannot say no to a dish of home-made stuffing
setter's reading: a person who compulsively crams the home full of possessions

explanation.walkthrough: Stuffing looks like the food in a roast; it is really the act of filling a house with things.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who compulsively accumulates and keeps possessions, unable to throw anything away, is this kind of collector.

clue.text: Point both ways

indicators.note: both ways says the word reads the same in either direction

blocks.note: to point someone to a source is to direct them there

explanation.definitionFit: To refer someone to something is to direct their attention there, just as pointing does.

clue.text: Deception linked with manufactured pop

indicators.note: linked suggests the two words are interlocked, their letters meshed into a new order

blocks.note: a lie is a deception
manufactured goods are made

explanation.surface: A deceit tied to a factory-produced soft drink.
explanation.walkthrough: The two words interlock: L, I and the second E come from the deception word, threaded around M, A, D and E.
explanation.definitionFit: Pop is an informal word for a fizzy soft drink, and limeade is a sweet citrus one.

clue.text: Stagger away, say, quickly

blocks.note: to reel is to stagger unsteadily
off means away, as in going off

explanation.surface: Someone lurches off and quickly speaks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' looks like the usual signal for an example, but here it is the verb meaning speak.
explanation.definitionFit: To reel off a list is to recite it rapidly and fluently, saying the items one after another without pause.

clue.text: Sleeping supporter seen in border station

blocks.note: a garden border is a flower bed
a post is a station, as in a sentry's post

explanation.surface: A dozing fan spotted at a frontier checkpoint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Border station' looks like a frontier checkpoint; split it, so border is a garden bed.
explanation.definitionFit: A bedpost is one of the upright corner posts of a bed frame, holding up the place where someone sleeps.

clue.text: Dr Foster maybe, carer, repeatedly tracks cases of medicine round hospital

indicators.note: cases are the outer casing, so only the first and last letters of medicine are kept
round means surrounding, so the second railway goes around the hospital letter

blocks.note: a nurse is a carer
RY is the abbreviation for railway, the tracks, taken twice
H is the abbreviation for hospital
first and last letters of medicine

explanation.surface: A GP, a nurse, and repeated doses of medicine at a hospital.
explanation.walkthrough: Doctor Foster went to Gloucester is a traditional English children's verse, so the medical-sounding name is a red herring.
explanation.definitionFit: Doctor Foster is the subject of a traditional children's verse, an example of a short rhyming song for youngsters.
